title: Normal Operation - Standby
shortDescription: A single slow LED flash on the Carrier defrost control indicates normal standby.
fullDescription:
Carrier heat pumps display diagnostic codes via a blinking LED on the outdoor defrost control board. A single slow flash means the board is healthy, powered, and awaiting a call for heating or cooling.

No action is needed. This code is a reassurance that the control board, 24V supply, and microprocessor are all functional.
symptoms: Single slow flash on outdoor LED

fixSteps.title: No action
fixSteps.instruction: This is normal. If system still doesn't run, verify thermostat setting and batteries.

whenToCallPro: Not required.

faq.a: One flash is normal standby - not an error.

title: No 24VAC to Defrost Control
shortDescription: The defrost board is not receiving 24V from the indoor unit.
fullDescription:
Two flashes indicate loss of 24VAC at the outdoor defrost board. This power comes from the indoor air handler/furnace through the low-voltage thermostat wire (R terminal).

Causes include a blown 3A fuse on the indoor board, broken thermostat wire, or a failed transformer.
safetyWarning: Check for shorted thermostat wires before replacing the fuse to avoid damage.

causes.cause: Blown 3A fuse on indoor control board
Broken low-voltage wire at outdoor unit

fixSteps.title: Check indoor fuse
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect and replace the 3A automotive-style fuse on the indoor board.

fixSteps.title: Measure 24V
fixSteps.instruction: Check 24VAC between R and C at outdoor terminal block.

whenToCallPro: If fuse repeatedly blows or transformer replacement is needed.

faq.a: Usually a shorted thermostat wire or chafed outdoor wire against metal.

title: Pressure Switch Open / Refrigerant Problem
shortDescription: High or low pressure switch has opened, stopping the compressor.
fullDescription:
Three flashes mean the defrost board sees an open pressure switch - either the high pressure switch tripped (head pressure too high) or the low pressure switch tripped (loss of charge).

High pressure faults usually stem from dirty condenser coil or restricted airflow. Low pressure points to refrigerant loss.
safetyWarning: Do not bypass pressure switches.

fixSteps.title: Clean condenser
fixSteps.instruction: Wash fins with water.

fixSteps.title: Verify outdoor fan
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm the fan spins whenever compressor runs.

fixSteps.title: Call for leak test
fixSteps.instruction: If low pressure suspected, schedule pro for leak search.

whenToCallPro: For refrigerant leaks.

faq.a: Check the switch bodies - HPS is usually red/yellow, LPS blue.

title: Limit Switch / Loss of Charge
shortDescription: Compressor limit switch open or loss of charge detected.
fullDescription:
Four flashes indicate the compressor internal overload limit has tripped or the low-charge protection has detected loss of refrigerant.

Allow the compressor to cool (30 minutes) and check refrigerant pressures. Frequent trips require pro diagnostics.

fixSteps.title: Cool down
fixSteps.instruction: Turn off for 30 minutes.

fixSteps.title: Check airflow
fixSteps.instruction: Clean filter and outdoor coil.

fixSteps.title: Charge check
fixSteps.instruction: Have a pro verify refrigerant charge.

whenToCallPro: For refrigerant and charge diagnostics.

faq.a: Yes, brownouts can overheat the compressor.

title: Thermistor Fault (Outdoor Temperature Sensor)
shortDescription: Outdoor ambient or coil thermistor is open or shorted.
fullDescription:
Five flashes signal a thermistor circuit problem. Carrier defrost boards use a 10k ohm ambient and 10k ohm coil thermistor to manage defrost cycles.

Without valid readings the board cannot control defrost correctly and may lock out.

fixSteps.title: Power off outdoor
fixSteps.instruction: Open disconnect.

fixSteps.title: Reseat thermistor
fixSteps.instruction: Find 2-pin thermistor plug on the defrost board and reseat.

fixSteps.title: Measure resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Should be ~10k ohms at 25C.

whenToCallPro: Only if board itself is defective.

faq.a: Cooling may work but defrost will be unreliable.

title: Low Line Voltage
shortDescription: Outdoor unit detected line voltage below acceptable range.
fullDescription:
Six flashes mean the defrost board measured the incoming line voltage and found it below the minimum safe level (typically <197V on a 208/230V system).

The compressor will not run to prevent damage. Check the supply service, disconnect, and contactor.

causes.cause: Loose wire at disconnect or contactor

fixSteps.title: Measure voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Verify 208-230V at the disconnect with unit off.

fixSteps.title: Inspect lugs
fixSteps.instruction: Check for loose or corroded terminal lugs.

whenToCallPro: For utility issues or wire sizing concerns.

faq.a: Yes if your whole house measures low voltage.

title: Compressor Stuck / Seized
shortDescription: Compressor did not start when commanded.
fullDescription:
Seven flashes indicate that the contactor closed but the compressor did not draw current (or drew massive lock-rotor current). Causes include a failed run capacitor, seized compressor, or open motor winding.

A capacitor test is the first step - many 7-flash faults are simply a weak run cap.
safetyWarning: Capacitors store lethal charge - discharge safely before handling.
symptoms: Hum from compressor but no run

fixSteps.title: Power off
fixSteps.instruction: Shut outdoor disconnect and discharge capacitor with insulated screwdriver.

fixSteps.title: Test capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: Measure uF - should be within 6% of nameplate.

fixSteps.title: Replace if needed
fixSteps.instruction: Swap capacitor matching microfarad and voltage rating.

whenToCallPro: If capacitor is fine - compressor replacement is costly.

faq.q: How do I tell if capacitor or compressor is bad?
faq.a: If the compressor hums and draws high current but won't start, test the capacitor first.

title: Reversing Valve Stuck
shortDescription: Defrost board cannot verify reversing valve position.
fullDescription:
Eight flashes mean the defrost board expected a reversing valve change (into or out of defrost) but didn't detect the coil temperature response. The valve may be stuck or the coil sensor may be misreading.

Check the O/B wire at the outdoor terminal and verify the reversing valve solenoid is energized in the correct mode.
symptoms: No heat or no cool despite compressor running

fixSteps.title: Verify O/B wire
fixSteps.instruction: Check voltage on O wire - should be 24V in cooling mode for Carrier.

fixSteps.title: Test solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Measure solenoid coil resistance.

whenToCallPro: For valve replacement (requires brazing and refrigerant recovery).

faq.q: Can I tap the valve to unstick?
faq.a: Light taps with a rubber mallet sometimes free a stuck slug - pros do this first.

title: Secondary Voltage Fuse Blown
shortDescription: The outdoor 24V fuse on the defrost board is blown.
fullDescription:
Nine flashes indicate the fuse protecting the 24V circuit on the outdoor defrost board itself has blown. This protects against short circuits in the outdoor low-voltage wiring.

Commonly caused by a contactor coil short, chafed thermostat wire, or failed reversing valve solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Find the fuse
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect board for 3A fuse.

fixSteps.title: Inspect for shorts
fixSteps.instruction: Check wires for chafing and coils for shorts BEFORE replacing fuse.

whenToCallPro: If cause isn't obvious.

faq.q: Can I replace the fuse with a larger one?
faq.a: No - it's sized to protect the board.

title: Low Pressure Lockout
shortDescription: Low pressure switch has tripped multiple times - lockout engaged.
fullDescription:
After repeated low pressure trips (typically three within an hour) the defrost board locks out with ten flashes. This protects the compressor from repeatedly starting against a lost refrigerant charge.

Manual reset is required - usually by cycling power - and the underlying leak must be found.
symptoms: Unit locked out, manual reset needed

fixSteps.title: Power cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Cut breaker 5 minutes to reset.

fixSteps.title: Call for leak search
fixSteps.instruction: Do not add refrigerant - a pro must find the leak.

whenToCallPro: Always.

faq.q: Will it come back after reset?
faq.a: Yes - the leak will cause it to trip again.

title: High Fire / Lockout (Infinity/Evolution)
shortDescription: Infinity-series heat pump locked out due to repeated protection events.
fullDescription:
HF (High Fire) on Infinity/Evolution heat pumps indicates the system has locked out after multiple high-pressure or high-temperature protection trips.

On communicating systems, check the Infinity touchscreen history for the original fault that caused lockout.

fixSteps.title: Check history
fixSteps.instruction: Use Infinity thermostat fault history menu.

fixSteps.title: Clean coils/filter
fixSteps.instruction: Restore airflow before resetting.

fixSteps.title: Reset system
fixSteps.instruction: Cycle main breaker.

whenToCallPro: If fault returns after cleaning.

faq.q: Is HF the same as a flash code?
faq.a: It's the communicating-system equivalent for chronic protection trips.

title: Low Heat Lockout
shortDescription: Infinity system has locked out heating due to repeated low-pressure/charge events.
fullDescription:
LH on Infinity/Evolution systems indicates the heat pump has disabled heating mode after repeated low-side faults. Emergency heat via backup strips may still run.

The underlying cause is usually loss of charge.
symptoms: Aux heat running but heat pump not

fixSteps.title: Use aux heat temporarily
fixSteps.instruction: Set thermostat to Emergency Heat until service.

fixSteps.title: Schedule pro visit
fixSteps.instruction: Leak search and charge repair.

whenToCallPro: Always.

faq.q: Why does aux heat still work?
faq.a: It's a separate electric heater independent of the compressor.

title: Indoor Air Handler Communication Lost
shortDescription: The Infinity system cannot reach the indoor unit.
fullDescription:
E1 on Carrier Infinity systems indicates that the User Interface (thermostat) cannot communicate with the indoor air handler or furnace. All Infinity devices share 4 wires (ABCD) and rely on continuous digital communication.

Check wiring continuity, correct color assignment, and indoor unit power.

fixSteps.title: Verify wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm A-A, B-B, C-C, D-D across thermostat and indoor board.

fixSteps.title: Power cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Turn indoor breaker off 5 minutes.

whenToCallPro: For board replacement.

faq.q: Can I use regular thermostat wire?
faq.a: Yes - 18/4 or 18/5 is fine; color matters less than continuity.

title: Outdoor Unit Communication Lost
shortDescription: Infinity UI has lost communication with the heat pump outdoor unit.
fullDescription:
E2 indicates the Infinity thermostat can talk to the indoor unit but not the outdoor. Communication to the outdoor rides on the same ABCD bus plus Y/Y2/O connections depending on the model.

Check wiring from indoor to outdoor and outdoor power.

fixSteps.title: Check outdoor power
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm disconnect and breaker on.

fixSteps.title: Verify wire
fixSteps.instruction: Check ABCD continuity between indoor and outdoor.

whenToCallPro: For control board issues.

faq.a: Sometimes wet terminals cause intermittent E2 - inspect after storms.

title: Outdoor Sensor Fault
shortDescription: Outdoor temperature sensor is open, shorted, or out of range.
fullDescription:
E3 on Infinity heat pumps indicates the outdoor ambient temperature sensor is reading an invalid value. This sensor is used for defrost and balance-point calculations.

Many Infinity models use a dedicated 10k thermistor mounted near the outdoor coil intake.

fixSteps.title: Power off outdoor
fixSteps.instruction: Switch disconnect.

fixSteps.title: Reseat and test
fixSteps.instruction: Reseat sensor plug and measure ~10k ohms at 25C.

whenToCallPro: Only if sensor replacement doesn't fix it.

faq.a: It's primarily a winter/defrost sensor but also used for efficiency calculations.

title: System Lockout - Hard Lockout
shortDescription: Heat pump locked out due to repeated safety trips.
fullDescription: A hard lockout on a Carrier Infinity/Performance heat pump occurs when the system has tripped a safety multiple times in a row (typically 4 trips within an hour). The control prevents further operation until manually reset to avoid equipment damage.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.

fixSteps.title: Reset Power
fixSteps.instruction: Switch breaker off for 1 minute and back on to clear the lockout.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Outdoor Unit
fixSteps.instruction: Look for ice on coil, blocked airflow, or visible damage.

fixSteps.title: Check Air Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Replace clogged indoor filter that can cause low-pressure trips.

fixSteps.title: Call HVAC Pro
fixSteps.instruction: If lockout returns, refrigerant charge or pressure switch needs evaluation.

repairTime: 15 minutes for reset; 1-3 hours for diagnosis
whenToCallPro: If lockout recurs after reset, professional diagnosis is required to find the underlying safety trip.

faq.q: What does a hard lockout mean?
faq.a: It means the control has tripped its safety four times in an hour and refuses to retry until reset.
Only temporarily if the underlying issue (refrigerant, pressure, airflow) is not resolved.

faq.q: Is it safe to keep resetting?
faq.a: No. Repeated lockouts indicate a real fault that can damage the compressor.

title: Defrost Mode Active
shortDescription: Heat pump in defrost cycle - normal operation.
fullDescription: Eleven flashes on the LED indicates the Carrier heat pump is in defrost mode. The reversing valve switches to cooling temporarily to melt frost from the outdoor coil. This is normal in cold weather but excessive defrost may indicate problems.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Brief blow of cool air indoors

fixSteps.title: Observe Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Defrost should last 2-10 minutes then return to heating.

fixSteps.title: Clear Snow
fixSteps.instruction: Remove snow/ice from around outdoor unit and on top of coil.

fixSteps.title: Check Frequency
fixSteps.instruction: If defrost runs more than every 30 min, call a technician.

whenToCallPro: If defrost cycles run more frequently than every 30 minutes or last over 10 minutes, call a pro.

faq.a: Yes. Heat pumps build frost in cold humid weather and must defrost periodically.

faq.q: Why does it blow cool air?
faq.a: The reversing valve flips during defrost; aux heat usually offsets this.
Typically every 30-90 minutes in below-freezing weather.

title: Outdoor Sensor Fault
shortDescription: Outdoor air temperature sensor open or shorted.
fullDescription: Twelve flashes indicate the outdoor temperature sensor is reading out of range. The control uses this sensor for defrost timing and balance-point staging, so a fault degrades efficiency and may force backup heat.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Aux heat runs more than usual

fixSteps.title: Locate Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find the small thermistor mounted on the outdoor unit cabinet.

fixSteps.title: Check Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness from sensor to control board for chew damage.

fixSteps.title: Measure Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect and read sensor; should be 10-30 kΩ at outdoor temps.

fixSteps.title: Replace Sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Swap with manufacturer part if out of spec.

whenToCallPro: If wiring is good and the sensor reads correctly, the control board may need service.

faq.a: Yes, but it defaults to fixed defrost timing and may use more aux heat.
Yes, it is a screw-in thermistor with a two-wire connector.
$25-$60 depending on model.

title: Limit Circuit Fault
shortDescription: Indoor limit switch tripped on heat pump backup heat.
fullDescription: Thirteen flashes show the indoor blower's limit switch opened due to overheating in the air handler. On heat pumps with electric strip heat, this often points to airflow problems while aux heat is energized.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Blower keeps running after heat off

fixSteps.title: Replace Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install new high-flow filter.

fixSteps.title: Open Registers
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm all supply and return vents are unblocked.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Blower
fixSteps.instruction: Verify wheel spins freely and motor runs at full speed.

fixSteps.title: Test Sequencers
fixSteps.instruction: Pro should check heat strip sequencers and contactor.

whenToCallPro: If airflow is fine but the limit keeps tripping, the heat strips or sequencers need a pro.

faq.a: Insufficient airflow can't carry away heat from the strip elements.
Most are auto-reset; if manual, only a pro should reset after diagnosis.
Never. It is a fire-safety device.

title: Reversing Valve Fault
shortDescription: Reversing valve failed to switch correctly.
fullDescription: Fourteen flashes report that the reversing valve did not change state when commanded. The heat pump may be stuck in cooling or heating regardless of thermostat call.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Outdoor unit runs but indoor air wrong

fixSteps.title: Verify Mode
fixSteps.instruction: Check thermostat is set to correct mode (heat or cool).

fixSteps.title: Listen for Click
fixSteps.instruction: Solenoid should click loudly when mode changes.

fixSteps.title: Test Solenoid Power
fixSteps.instruction: Measure 24V at solenoid coil during mode change.

fixSteps.title: Call Tech
fixSteps.instruction: Valve replacement requires recovery and brazing.

whenToCallPro: Reversing valve replacement is a refrigerant-circuit job and must be done by a certified tech.

faq.q: Can a stuck valve be tapped free?
faq.a: Sometimes a tech can free a stuck slide by cycling power; otherwise replacement is needed.
$700-$1500 typically including refrigerant work.
Often yes if the system is under 10 years old.

title: High-Pressure Switch Open
shortDescription: High-pressure switch tripped on outdoor unit.
fullDescription: Fifteen flashes indicate the high-pressure switch opened, shutting down the compressor to protect it from dangerously high discharge pressure. Common in cooling mode with airflow problems.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Outdoor fan may not be running

fixSteps.title: Wash Coil
fixSteps.instruction: Spray outdoor coil with garden hose top-down to remove debris.

fixSteps.title: Check Fan
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm outdoor fan spins freely and runs at full RPM.

fixSteps.title: Clear Vegetation
fixSteps.instruction: Maintain 24" clearance around the unit.

fixSteps.title: Pro Diagnosis
fixSteps.instruction: Have technician verify charge and condenser airflow.

whenToCallPro: If the unit trips again after cleaning, charge or fan capacitor needs professional evaluation.

faq.a: Without airflow over the coil, refrigerant cannot reject heat and pressure spikes.
Often yes if the coil was very dirty; check fan capacitor too.
Yes, sustained high pressure can damage the compressor.

title: Low-Pressure Switch Open
shortDescription: Low-pressure switch tripped - low refrigerant suspected.
fullDescription: Sixteen flashes signal the low-pressure switch opened, indicating very low suction pressure. This usually means a refrigerant leak, blocked indoor airflow, or an extremely cold outdoor temperature in heating.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.

fixSteps.title: Replace Filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install a fresh filter and run blower-only to thaw any ice.

fixSteps.title: Check Coil
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect indoor coil for frost or dirt buildup.

fixSteps.title: Listen for Hiss
fixSteps.instruction: A leak may be audible near connections.

fixSteps.title: Call Pro
fixSteps.instruction: Leak search and recharge require certification.

whenToCallPro: Low refrigerant always means a leak; topping off without repair is bad practice and illegal in many regions.

faq.a: Vibration, corrosion, or factory defects in joints over time.
EPA certification is required to handle refrigerant.
Usually yes, but sometimes the coil must be replaced.

title: Suction Pressure Sensor Fault
shortDescription: Pressure transducer reporting out of range.
fullDescription: On Infinity-series Carrier heat pumps, seventeen flashes indicate the suction-line pressure transducer is reading invalid values. The control cannot stage the variable-speed compressor accurately.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.
symptoms: Variable-speed unit runs at fixed stage

fixSteps.title: Power Cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Reset breaker for 60 seconds.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Connector
fixSteps.instruction: Reseat the 3-pin transducer connector.

fixSteps.title: Check Wire
fixSteps.instruction: Look for chafing along harness route.

fixSteps.title: Replace Transducer
fixSteps.instruction: Schrader-mount transducers swap without recovery in some models.

whenToCallPro: Most transducers are on a Schrader port but some require recovery - call a tech if unsure.

faq.a: Yes, in a fallback fixed-stage mode at lower efficiency.
$60-$150 for the part.
Internal diaphragm fatigue or moisture intrusion at the connector.

title: Compressor Inrush Failure
shortDescription: Compressor failed to start on multiple attempts.
fullDescription: Eighteen flashes mean the inverter or contactor attempted to start the compressor but locked-rotor was sensed. The control aborts to prevent burnout.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.

fixSteps.title: Check Voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Verify 240V at the disconnect with multimeter.

fixSteps.title: Test Capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: Discharge and read capacitance against label rating.

fixSteps.title: Replace Cap
fixSteps.instruction: Install new dual run capacitor if weak.

fixSteps.title: Call Pro
fixSteps.instruction: If cap is good, compressor may be seized.

whenToCallPro: Replace the capacitor first - a seized compressor is a major repair and may justify replacement.

faq.a: No, $20-$60 typically.

faq.q: How do I know the compressor is seized?
faq.a: It hums loudly without spinning and trips the breaker quickly.
Compressor replacement on older units is often not worth it.

title: Low Stage Pressure Switch Open
shortDescription: Low-stage pressure switch tripped on two-stage compressor.
fullDescription: Nineteen flashes are reported on Carrier two-stage heat pumps when the low-stage pressure switch trips, often due to airflow loss specifically during low-stage operation.
safetyWarning: Always disconnect power at the breaker before opening any HVAC equipment. High-voltage circuits and refrigerant systems can cause serious injury.

causes.cause: Frozen indoor coil at low load

symptoms: System ramps to high stage immediately

fixSteps.title: Replace Filter
fixSteps.instruction: New filter and confirm blower speed.

fixSteps.title: Check Registers
fixSteps.instruction: Open all supply registers to maximize airflow.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Coil
fixSteps.instruction: Look for frost or dust buildup.

fixSteps.title: Pro Service
fixSteps.instruction: If repeats, refrigerant charge needs verification.

whenToCallPro: If filter and airflow are fine, refrigerant or pressure switch evaluation is needed.

faq.a: Yes, Performance and Infinity series use two-stage compressors.
Yes in high stage but at lower efficiency.
Lower mass flow can't handle marginal restrictions that high stage masks.

title: Defrost Thermostat Stuck Closed
shortDescription: Defrost sensor reads as if always cold.
fullDescription: The defrost thermostat is mechanically stuck or its wiring shorted, causing the unit to attempt defrost continuously.
safetyWarning: Turn off power at the breaker before opening the unit. HVAC systems contain high-voltage components and refrigerant under pressure.

causes.cause: Loose wiring or connector at terminal block
Sensor or thermistor out of calibration

symptoms: 20 flashes displayed on diagnostic LED or controller
Unit will not start or shuts down quickly
Indoor or outdoor fan behavior abnormal

fixSteps.title: Power Reset
fixSteps.instruction: Switch off the breaker for 5 minutes, then restore power and observe whether the code returns.

fixSteps.title: Visual Inspection
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, open the service panel and inspect connectors, sensor leads, and contactors for damage or looseness.

fixSteps.title: Call Technician
fixSteps.instruction: If the fault persists after a reset and visual check, contact a licensed HVAC technician for component-level diagnosis.

repairTime: 30 minutes to 3 hours depending on root cause
whenToCallPro: Call a licensed HVAC technician if a power reset and basic inspection do not clear the fault, or any time refrigerant or sealed-system work is required.

faq.a: Only the power reset and visual checks are DIY-safe; component diagnosis or refrigerant work requires a licensed technician.
Typical service calls run $150-$500; sealed-system or compressor work can exceed $1,500.
If the unit is not heating or cooling at all, treat it as urgent. If it self-recovers, schedule service soon to prevent recurrence.

fixSteps.title: Call Technician
fixSteps.instruction: If the fault persists after a reset and visual check, contact a licensed HVAC technician for component-level diagnosis.

repairTime: 30 minutes to 3 hours depending on root cause
whenToCallPro: Call a licensed HVAC technician if a power reset and basic inspection do not clear the fault, or any time refrigerant or sealed-system work is required.

faq.a: Only the power reset and visual checks are DIY-safe; component diagnosis or refrigerant work requires a licensed technician.
Typical service calls run $150-$500; sealed-system or compressor work can exceed $1,500.
If the unit is not heating or cooling at all, treat it as urgent. If it self-recovers, schedule service soon to prevent recurrence.
